units.label: Title: Weather Fronts and Storm Formation
Hook: satellite storm image (image)
units.content_summary: Satellite photo of a large spiral storm system over land, with a visible boundary line where cloud cover changes abruptly. Caption: 'What causes this sharp line in the clouds?'

units.label: Learning Objectives (text)
units.content_summary: Objectives: define a weather front; distinguish the four front types; explain why fronts cause precipitation; describe how fronts relate to storm formation.

units.label: Definition: front (text)
units.content_summary: A front is the boundary between two air masses of different temperature and humidity. Fronts are where most significant weather changes and precipitation occur, since warm and cold air do not mix easily.

units.label: Cold front diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Cross-section diagram of a cold front: dense cold air wedges under warm air, forcing it up sharply, producing narrow bands of intense thunderstorms.

units.label: Warm front diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Cross-section diagram of a warm front: warm air gradually rises over retreating cold air along a shallow slope, producing widespread, lighter, longer-lasting precipitation.

units.label: Occluded and stationary fronts (text)
units.content_summary: Occluded front: a cold front catches up to a warm front, lifting the warm air completely off the ground. Stationary front: two air masses meet but neither advances, causing prolonged rain in one area for days.

units.label: Weather map symbols (image)
units.content_summary: Standard weather map symbols for the four front types: blue triangles (cold), red semicircles (warm), alternating triangles/semicircles (occluded), alternating on opposite sides (stationary).

units.label: Storm formation at fronts (text)
units.content_summary: When warm moist air is forced upward at a front, it cools and condenses, releasing energy that fuels storm development. Cold fronts, with their steep lifting, tend to produce the most severe storms including thunderstorms and occasionally tornadoes.

units.label: Video: front passage timelapse (video)
units.content_summary: Timelapse video showing clouds building and a thunderstorm developing as a cold front passes through, followed by clearing skies and a noticeable temperature drop.

units.label: Real-world application: forecasting (text)
units.content_summary: Meteorologists track fronts on weather maps to forecast upcoming precipitation and temperature changes. A cold front approaching typically means an incoming temperature drop and possible severe weather within hours.

units.label: Practice questions (text)
units.content_summary: Four questions: identify a front type from its map symbol; explain why cold fronts produce more intense storms than warm fronts; describe what happens at an occluded front; predict weather given an approaching front type.
